newsitem.title: USA: Clinton aides signal tough work ahead on budget.
newsitem.headline: Clinton aides signal tough work ahead on budget.

text.p: White House officials said Saturday they were optimistic about working out final details of the 2002 balanced budget agreement with Congress, although they signalled that hard work remained to be done.

Gene Sperling, a top economic aide to President Clinton and chairman of the National Economic Council, told CNN's "Evans & Novak" there were "some tough issues that still need to be resolved," and White House negotiators should be "willing to walk if suddenly there's bad faith."
"It's going to be rough sledding at every stage," Sperling said, citing differences over tax cuts and other issues, although he did not expect last week's budget deal to unravel.

"I think what you have is a week of ironing out some differences," Sperling said of efforts to flesh out the agreement. "I'm quite confident that we will have a more formal agreement over the next few days."

Republicans and Democrats this week resorted to quibbling over what the May 2 budget agreement actually included, and House budget and tax leaders cast doubt upon whether the pact had specified the $35 billion in education tax credits over five years that Clinton was seeking for college tuition.
The budget agreement provided for a gross $135 billion tax cut over five years offset by $50 billion in tax increases for a net tax cut of $85 billion.

White House spokesman Michael McCurry, in Barbados with Clinton for a summit of Caribbean nations, told CNN's "Inside Politics Weekend" it was up to congressional tax-writing committees to write the tax bills, not the negotiators.
He reiterated that House Speaker Newt Gingrich and Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott agreed to the $35 billion in education tax credits.
"That is a commitment, and the majority leader of the Senate and the speaker of the House know that that is a commitment," he said.

"A deal's a deal and we're going to make sure that those things that were in the agreement -- the framework agreement that was put together by the White House and by congressional negotiators -- hold up in the end of the day," McCurry said.
"But it's a very, very complicated budget agreement, and implementing it now will take a lot of hard work," he said.

Asked if the deal could still fall apart, he said, "It could unravel only if the majority leader and the speaker don't remind their congressional committee chairs that an agreement has been struck here with the president."
Less optimistic that Sperling, McCurry predicted that "wrangling over the details" could take weeks, not days.

Sperling acknowledged that all the details of the May 2 budget deal were not recorded on paper and that negotiators were still discussing specific domestic spending priorities. He described the administration's agreement to a cut in the capital gains tax as a concesssion.

He supported a Republican proposal to allow tax-free withdrawals from Individual Retirement Accounts (IRAs) for educational purposes, but would not say that this proposal would be part of the $35 billion that Clinton was seeking to fund his Hope Scholarship and $10,000 educational deduction.
Sperling said the budget deal "gives both sides something to brag about" and predicted a majority of Democrats in the House would support it.
He said some items proposed might have to be phased in, rather than take effect immediately, possibly including any changes in IRA withdrawals.

He said the administration did not favour Republican proposals to index for inflation of capital gains, since it might encourage formation of tax shelters, but he did not rule out an agreement on this issue.
